extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers interested in Madeleine L'Engle and advice on writing for children
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and authorial principles for writing books for children, drawn from Madeleine L'Engle's remarks and practice; includes advice about voice, subject matter, and the use of fantasy to convey difficult ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to intuitive understanding of childhood
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer of a good children's book may need to return to the 'intuitive understanding of his own childhood,' being 'childlike although not childish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L'Engle advises that effective children's writers reconnect with the imaginative perspective of childhood; this is about voice and sensibility rather than immature or simplistic writing. Aim for childlike openness without talking down to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make demands of child readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often possible to make demands of a child that couldn't be made of an adult; a child will often understand scientific concepts that would baffle an adult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L'Engle suggests that authors should not underestimate children's capacity for complex ideas — they can accept imaginative leaps and conceptual difficulty. Rather than oversimplifying, present challenging material framed through imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage the child's imaginative leap
rubrics_metrics.description: A child can understand with a 'leap of the imagination' that is denied the grown-up who has acquired knowledge that can close off imaginative possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative conceits and metaphors that allow young readers to grasp abstract or scientific themes; the writer's task is to invite that imaginative leap rather than substitute adult explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children come with an open mind — introduce philosophy and science
rubrics_metrics.description: Of philosophy, etc., as well as science, 'the child will come to it with an open mind, whereas many adults come closed to an open book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can introduce philosophical and scientific themes directly to children because young readers often approach ideas without the preconceptions adults hold. Present such subjects accessibly but without diluting their substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fantasy to say important and difficult things
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers turn to fantasy (which children claim as their own) when they have something important and difficult to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L'Engle recommends fantasy as a powerful vehicle for conveying complex moral, spiritual, or intellectual themes to children; employ fantastical elements intentionally to illuminate difficult topics rather than as mere escapism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as truth; blur fiction and memoir when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: For L'Engle, who wrote repeatedly about 'story as truth', the distinction between fiction and memoir was sometimes blurred; real events from her life and family history made their way into some of her novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using personal experience as material for fiction to convey emotional truth. Blending autobiographical elements with invented ones can strengthen authenticity and resonance in children's (and adult) fiction, but maintain clarity about the story's form as needed for audience expectations.
